title: Building a Black Honors Community
description: The inaugural class of Sacramento State’s Black Honors College poses with campus leaders at a ceremony. When Naomi Thrower was applying to college, she knew she wanted the historically Black college or university experience but hesitated to leave the community she had built in California, which does not have a traditional HBCU. So she applied to HBCUs across the country, as well as to California State University, Sacramento , the state’s first Black-serving institution . “Sacramento State is the only California school I applied to. The rest were all East Coast HBCUs,” Thrower said. “I do have family on the East Coast, but none I felt strongly connected with. So I would be leaving my family, my friends, the life I’ve built here, and that was a little nerve-racking.” Now a fourth-year deaf studies major, Thrower has found a community in the university’s Black Honors College , a first-of-its-kind program that provides a culturally responsive curriculum and inclusive academic community for students focused on the Black experience.

title: The Future of the American University, According to Cornell Faculty
description: The Cornell provost convened a faculty committee to explore how the university should change over the next 50 years and adapt to the rise of generative artificial intelligence and eroding public trust in higher education. As higher education contends with seismic upheaval, the university cannot remain “exactly as it is today,” faculty at Cornell University said in a new report that outlines how the Ivy League institution can weather the current storms and “prepare for those that we cannot yet predict.” The report resembles attempts from faculty at Vanderbilt and Yale Universities to diagnose what ails higher education and to chart a course forward. Unlike the Yale and Vanderbilt reports, the Cornell faculty largely contained their discussion to their own university, though they noted that they hope the commitments and recommendations inspire other institutions. Cornell Provost Kavita Bala convened an interdisciplinary committee of faculty last fall to explore how the university should change over the next 50 years and specifically adapt to three disruptions: rapid technological change, fissures in the relationship between universities and the federal government, and the erosion of public trust in higher education. The results of that 18-person committee’s work were released Tuesday in a 238-page report and a condensed 17-page vision statement . “The committee’s central premise is that the wave of disruption challenging higher education today is not a passing threat driven by transient forces,” the panel wrote in the vision statement . “Tensions between universities and the federal government are symptoms of larger, longer-term systemic issues that have arisen over decades. The future of the American university lies in leadership that recommits to a clear purpose, which the committee defines as promoting a human-centered, integrated learning ecosystem to cultivate sound judgment.”

title: Colleges Adopted ‘Systemic Suppression’ of Protesters, New Investigation Shows
description: A California Highway Patrol officer arrests a protester on May 2, 2024, while clearing a pro-Palestinian encampment at the University of California, Los Angeles. Government officials and university administrators took “heavy-handed” and “excessive” actions in response to campus protests after Oct. 7, 2023, actions that “disproportionately targeted” pro-Palestinian students and faculty members, creating a chilling effect that will stifle political expression for years to come, a new report says . Produced by the American Civil Liberties Union and Amnesty International USA, the 287-page report documents what it calls the “systemic suppression” of anti-genocide speech at colleges and universities across the country. The “McCarthyite censorship” against individuals who exercised their right to free speech and criticized the Israeli government for the nation’s protracted war in Gaza continues to this day, the authors argue. “Universities’ responses to campus-related Palestine advocacy and pro-Palestinian demonstrations have been more punitive in comparison with their historical responses to other comparable demonstrations over decades,” the report says. As a result, “These universities directly or indirectly have made it easier for the Trump administration to crack down on student activism, causing long-term damage to higher education.” Based on a two-year investigation, the report covers events, policies and practices that have unfolded since the terror attacks of Oct. 7 at 80 public and private colleges and universities across 28 states and Washington, D.C. It draws on college records, statements from government agencies and officials, court records, case law, media reports, and survey responses from students who participated in protests at 41 colleges. (Ninety-six individuals completed the survey.)

title: ED Redirects $235M in MSI Funds to HBCUs, Tribal Colleges
description: McMahon said, “For nearly 200 years, HBCUs have been engines of opportunity.” The Education Department announced Tuesday that it is sending more than $174 million to historically Black colleges and universities and $61 million to tribal colleges. It says the “one-time” investments come from programs that generally funded Hispanic-serving and other minority-serving institutions—the same way it provided a similar boost to HBCUs and tribal colleges last year. Last September, ED abruptly canceled grants for most minority-serving institutions, saying those programs were unconstitutionally discriminatory because they require colleges to enroll a certain percentage of students from a particular racial or ethnic background to qualify. ED then redirected $495 million to HBCUs and tribal colleges. In December, the Justice Department backed up ED’s legal interpretation. On Tuesday, ED told Inside Higher Ed that it has urged Congress to fix the constitutional issues, and for now it has worked with the White House Office of Management and Budget to identify legal options for the funds. Congress blocked the department from defunding the MSI programs entirely, but it allowed the agency to move the money into the Strengthening Institutions Program. This year, the money for HBCUs is from a grant program for Hispanic-serving institutions aimed at boosting the number of Hispanic and low-income students in the STEM fields and developing model transfer and articulation agreements between two- and four-year institutions in such fields, the Education Department said. Tribal colleges are getting about $14.4 million from the STEM program.

title: Conn. State System Scandal Drives Demands for Reform
description: Maduko was the second CSCU system chancellor to leave in less than a year. Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | Connecticut Board of Regents | Connecticut State Colleges and Universities When Connecticut State Colleges and Universities Interim Chancellor John Maduko resigned in April after 10 months on the job, officials noted he stepped down amid an investigation into a policy violation. Now an independent report has revealed that the system failed to adequately respond to multiple allegations of sexually inappropriate conduct by Maduko toward women working in the system. The report also found that the board ignored basic vetting practices in elevating Maduko, who had previously served a roughly three-year stint as president of Connecticut State Community College. Maduko is the second chancellor to leave in less than a year. His predecessor, Terrence Cheng, exited the role in June 2025 after the Board of Regents refused to renew his contract following a report that he spent lavishly on meals, alcohol and chauffeured rides to his home in New York.

title: Out Now: 2026 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers
description: Provosts are confident in their role and their relationship with their president, according to the 2026 Inside Higher Ed /Hanover Research Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers , out today (N=376). But, like last year, resources are a sticking point. In 2026, not quite half of provosts (47 percent) say they have what they need to actually implement initiatives. Provosts nevertheless trend optimistic about their institutions’ futures, though 13 percent signal near-term threats to their colleges’ ability to carry out their academic missions and 18 percent signal active financial distress. On Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 2 p.m. Eastern, Inside Higher Ed will present a free webcast featuring expert panelists to discuss the survey findings and navigating academic leadership and opportunity amid constraint. Register for that conversation here , even if you can’t attend live. Download a free copy of the survey report—which includes more findings on federal policy; campus speech, well-being and inclusion; AI; academic freedom and tenure; and institutional effectiveness. Read more analysis of the data here . Regarding the future of higher education broadly, just a quarter of provosts (25 percent) are at least somewhat confident that the U.S. university research enterprise will remain strong over the next decade. This increases to 43 percent among public doctoral university provosts, despite their disproportionate experience with recent federal funding cuts, which is also reflected in the survey. In write-in comments about underappreciated challenges, provosts flag topics from doing more with less to student readiness levels. Wrote one provost: “How to be adaptable and responsive to a changing society with increasingly constrained resources.” Some also describe the slate of recent policy changes as unfunded mandates that are increasing compliance costs without increasing quality.

title: Commercialized Federal Research Has Generated Trillions, Study Finds
description: As of 2025, universities own about 60 percent of the patents issued on inventions benefiting from federal funding. The government holds about 9 percent. Federally funded research continues to yield big payoffs for the broader national economy, new data shows. Between 2021 and 2025, the commercialization of university and nonprofit research that benefited from federal funding added as much as $577 billion to gross economic output, $288 billion in gross domestic production and more than one million jobs, according to a report the Bayh-Dole Coalition published Tuesday. Those gains, the report argues, are the latest evidence of the success of the Bayh-Dole Act of 1980, which allows universities, not-for-profit corporations and small businesses to patent and commercialize federally funded inventions. Prior to the legislation, the federal government owned the intellectual property of any discoveries made with federal research dollars. It gave universities little incentive to find practical uses for inventions, and fewer than 5 percent of the 28,000 patents held by federal agencies pre-1980 had been licensed for use, according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office . Since 1980, the annual number of patents issued on inventions benefiting from federal funding increased more than 70-fold, according to the report. And while the federal government owned most such patents prior to Bayh-Dole’s enactment, by 2025 universities owned about 60 percent, compared to just 9 percent held by the federal government.

title: Higher Ed and the Tale of 2 News Feeds
description: labsas/iStock Unreleased/Getty Images Plus Americans have argued over the role of colleges almost as long as they have argued over the Republic itself. Thomas Jefferson founded the University of Virginia as a secular institution, which was in stark contrast to the religious ties defining nearly all other colleges at the time. During the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln signed the Morrill Act, redefining the nation’s commitment to higher education. After World War II, the GI Bill opened college doors to millions of veterans and helped build the modern American middle class while expanding the role of higher education in society. In every era, Americans have debated whom colleges should serve, what they should teach and what they owe the country. Those debates continue today, at a time when public opinion about higher education appears to be shifting. Gallup, most notably, has documented a much-discussed decline in public confidence in higher education during the past decade, particularly among Republicans. Explanations usually focus on rising tuition, doubts about value, campus politics and ideological conflict. Those factors undoubtedly matter. Yet they ignore an important question that very much is part of the story: Where do Americans get the information from which they form their judgments about colleges and universities? To help us answer this question, we turn to the Vanderbilt Television News Archive , which offers new and compelling evidence about that changing national conversation. Our analysis of data from the archive shows that Americans are receiving different stories about what is happening on our college campuses. Americans, in effect, have been watching the same institution, but through two different news feeds. The archive began recording the evening news broadcasts of ABC, CBS and NBC in 1968. It began recording evening broadcasts for CNN in 1995 and Fox News Channel in 2004. To capture the changed information environment, we conducted an AI-assisted content analysis between 2004 and 2025. This analysis identified 517 unique segments devoted to higher education across the evening news shows from the five networks, then classified them by network and tone. Television is no longer the central source of political information, but its changing coverage speaks to the larger fragmentation of Americans’ information environment (as we’ll address in more detail below).

title: College athletics rack up millions in deficits as Senate eyes oversight bill
description: The congressional chamber could vote this week on the Protect College Sports Act, a proposal intended to stabilize the shifting collegiate landscape. Major court cases and policy changes in recent years have ushered in a new era of revenue sharing between institutions and players and for athletes to make money off their names, images and likeness. Since then, many athletes have taken to transferring teams in search of better compensation and colleges are rushing to raise money through donations and game day fees to attract top prospects. Words and phrases like “chaos,” “wild west” and “unsustainable” have been thrown around to describe the state of play. U.S. senators have used some of that same language to describe the situation, as a bill that would limit revenue sharing and college athlete transfers, among other measures, comes closer to a vote. Last week, the body voted 74-24 to move the Protect College Sports Act closer to a final vote, which is expected as soon as this week. The proposed legislation has broad bipartisan backing, as well as support from a wide array of higher education and college sports stakeholders.

title: Faculty group wants to block UNL’s attempted return to AAU over program cuts

Last summer , he attributed the multimillion-dollar gap in the university's budget to insufficient state funding, declining tuition revenue and high inflation. “Despite our best efforts to live within our means, our revenue has not kept pace with expenses,” he said at the time . The university ultimately approved the elimination of four departments — educational administration; statistics; earth and atmospheric sciences; and textiles, merchandising and fashion design. The decision came despite prolonged faculty objections , including allegations of potential problems with the university’s data used to identify cuts.

title: Judge vacates anti-DEI directive that led to teacher training grant cuts
description: A federal judge ruled the U.S. Department of Education’s edict and cancellation of hundreds of millions in funds for teacher training programs was unlawful. The order from the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts stated that the Feb. 5, 2025, directive — entitled “Eliminating Discrimination and Fraud in Department Grant Awards” — was arbitrary, capricious and violated the Administrative Procedure Act. On Feb. 17, 2025, the department announced the TQP and SEED grant cuts , citing funded initiatives that held professional development workshops on dismantling racial bias and activities that required educators to take personal and institutional responsibility for systemic inequities. “The Department’s hasty implementation of the Directive over less than two weeks, the magnitude of the effects of the termination, as well as the lack of evidence of reasoned decisionmaking in the Administrative Record leave serious doubts as to the Department’s choice to adopt the Directive,” said Kelley in the Sept. 17 order. The Education Department did not say whether it would appeal Kelley’s decision as of Sept. 21 in a request for comment from K-12 Dive.

title: Why Sterling College faltered — and how some plan to keep its legacy alive
description: The environmentally focused Vermont college closed after enrollment declines took their toll, but some are moving to create an institute to house its legacy. Editor’s note: The College Closure Files is an occasional column chronicling why institutions shuttered and what lessons higher education leaders can glean from those shutdowns. Tucked away in Vermont’s Green Mountains, Sterling College began as a preparatory school before becoming a college roughly half a century ago. Always small, the environmentally focused Sterling provided students with hands-on outdoor and agricultural experiences. But post-COVID enrollment declines took their toll. The college closed following its spring term this year. Before it was a college, the institution that became Sterling was a boys’ preparatory school tucked away in Vermont’s remote Northeast Kingdom . Its “students wore coats and ties, played soccer and chess, studied French, history, and mathematics,” according to a 1983 article by Ann Ingerson, then a faculty member. T hey were also expected to work hard and, beginning in the 1960s, went on an extended outdoor expedition through Vermont’s backwoods called Bounder. Its transition to a college came partly in response to a demographic upheaval as the Baby Boomer generation advanced out of K-12 schooling.
